abstract: | 
 Young people come of age amid a growing tension between the meritocratic promise of schooling — that effort and talent determine life chances — and mounting evidence that family wealth and connections shape outcomes. How they navigate this tension remains poorly understood, partly because research tends to treat belief in meritocracy as a single attitude that young people either absorb or reject. Drawing on two-wave panel data from Chilean students aged 11–16 (Wave 1: N = 846; Wave 2: N = 662), collected in one of the world's most marketized and stratified educational systems, this article shows that young people hold considerably more differentiated orientations. They distinguish how rewards are allocated from how they should be, and endorsement of merit coexists with recognition of privilege rather than displacing it; indeed, those who perceive greater privilege express stronger — not weaker — demands that rewards should follow merit. These orientations are stable within individuals over a one-year window, permitting valid developmental comparisons. Yet the meaning young people attach to the claim that "effort is rewarded" is not equivalent across school stages: older students interpret it through a more critical, experience-laden frame, consistent with a progressive reality shock as accumulated schooling makes structural advantage harder to ignore. Rather than passive recipients of meritocratic ideology, young people emerge as active interpreters of institutional narratives about fairness, demanding merit-based fairness precisely where they perceive its absence. The article contributes a longitudinally validated multidimensional approach for studying how these orientations develop across youth in unequal educational contexts.
 \newline
 **Keywords**: Meritocracy · Schools · Measurement invariance · Socialization · Chile
